issues.body:

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
abuse of sweeping arbitrary tokens.

## Proof of Concept
The _rescueFunds function allows sweeping any tokens, when it should only allow sweeping of the underlying asset

## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps

- Remove the _tokenAddress parameter - no need to specify which token, only sweep underlying
- Add a check of getCashPrior() >= amount to ensure there are sufficient underlying funds

issues.title: `setDirectPrice` is vulnerable to sandwich attack
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/src/core/Oracles/ChainlinkOracle.sol#L115-L138


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In `ChainlinkOracle.sol` we have `setDirectPrice()`:
```solidity
function setDirectPrice(address asset, uint256 price) external onlyAdmin {
        emit PricePosted(asset, prices[asset], price, price);
        prices[asset] = price;
    }
```

This function `setDirectPrice()` allows the admin of the contract to manually set the price of a given asset. 

The problem here is when the price is updated an attacker can sandwich the update to gain a profit.

## Proof of Concept

A malicious actor can watch the mempool for calls `setDirectPrice()` and front run the call and take advantage of it and make a profit.

- Admin call `setDirectPrice()` and change the price of the asset.
- Malicious user watch the mempool and see the transaction and takes advantage of this by seeing the price that will appear and if it is profitable takes advantage by swapping the given asset for profit.

This also applies to the `setUnderlyingPrice()` function.

## Tools Used

Visual Studio Code

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

This is very difficult to prevent. Only use these functions as a last resort. It's best not to use these functions and trust the data that comes from Chainlink.


## Assessed type

MEV

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/fced18035107a345c31c9a9497d0da09105df4df/src/core/MultiRewardDistributor/MultiRewardDistributor.sol#L912


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Recursive calls from ```calculateNewIndex``` in ```MultiRewardDistributor``` will result in an infinite loop and out of gas errors, preventing tokens from being minted and rewards being sent to some users as ```disburseSupplierRewardsInternal``` will not be called.

## Proof of Concept
Summarizing the interactions that occur when a user calls mint: 

MToken -> Comptroller -> MultiRewardDistributor -> MToken


When calculating a new index in function ```calculateNewIndex```, there is a call to an internal 
sub_ function, passing in ```blockTimestamp``` and ```_currentTimestamp```


```
uint256 deltaTimestamps = sub_(blockTimestamp, uint256(_currentTimestamp));
```

However, the way the sub_ function is implemented, it will cause an infinite loop due
to the recursive call to itself, which will throw an out of gas error and any gas used will be lost.

```
    function sub_(uint a, uint b) pure internal returns (uint) {
        return sub_(a, b, "subtraction underflow");
    }
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

I would recommend adding a check to the sub_ function that prevents the recursive call when the condition is not met.

This is in line with the safeMath library implementation. (https://github.com/ConsenSysMesh/openzeppelin-solidity/blob/master/contracts/math/SafeMath.sol)

```
function sub_(uint a, uint b) pure internal returns (uint) {
    require(b <= a, "subtraction underflow");
    return a - b;
}

Race condition in approve function can lead to more funds than intended being transferred
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/src/core/MToken.sol#L159-L164


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The approve() function from MToken.sol contains a front-running vulnerability that allows a user to spend more tokens than he should.

## Proof of Concept
Lets take the following scenario:
1. Alice calls approve(Eve, 10). This permits Eve to spend 10 tokens from Alice.
2. Alice changes her mind and calls approve(Eve, 5) to only allow Eve to spend 5 of her tokens, instead of 10.
3. Eve sees Alice's transaction and sends her own transaction calling transferFrom(Alice, Eve, 10), submitting it with a higher gas price than Alice.
4. If Eve's transaction gets included in the block before Alice's is, 10 tokens from Alice will be transferred to Eve. Then, after Alice's transaction is included, Eve can call transferFrom again, this time with the newly approved 5 tokens.
5. As a consequence, Alice only wanted and expected Eve to spend 5 of her tokens, while in reality, because of the race condition vulnerability, Eve was able to take 15 of Alice's tokens.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
One solution is to forbid a call to approve if the previous approved tokens were not spent. This would prevent the race condition: require(allowances[Alice][Eve] == 0, "error");

Another solution is to add 2 function to increase and decrease the allowances. Check the OpenZeppelin ERC20 implementation: https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/v4.9.3/contracts/token/ERC20/ERC20.sol



## Assessed type

ERC20

incorrect liquidity values that undermine the risk checks and constraints of the protocol

getHypotheticalAccountLiquidityInternal does not handle snapshot errors properly. Specifically:

It calls MToken.getAccountSnapshot() to get the account's token balance, borrow balance, and exchange rate.
If getAccountSnapshot returns a non-zero error code, it immediately returns SNAPSHOT_ERROR without checking/fixing the invalid state.

-Return a specialized error code indicating which markets had issues

issues.title: Any extra reward tokens that accumulate in the contract remain locked there permanently.
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/fced18035107a345c31c9a9497d0da09105df4df/src/core/MultiRewardDistributor/MultiRewardDistributor.sol#L2-L1248


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Funds get locked in contract resulting to Loss of asset control, funds and increased costs to recover fund

## Proof of Concept
Reviewing the list of external and public functions, there is no withdraw() or reclaim() function:
2.  Scanning the contract code, there are no internal or private functions for withdrawals either.
3.  The _rescueFunds() function can only be called by the Comptroller admin, not the MultiRewardDistributor admin.

There are no modifiers like onlyAdmin that restrict access to a withdrawal function.
So in summary, the lack of any external withdrawal capability indicates there is no way to reclaim funds from this contract currently.

withdrawing excess tokens could be useful for the following reasons

- If configured emission speeds are too high, excess tokens build up in the contract. The admin may want to reclaim these.
- If reward emission is turned off, leftover tokens remain locked in the contract. There is no way to get these out.
- When upgrading the reward distributor to a new contract, excess tokens in the old contract remain locked. There is no way to migrate them.
- If the emission token is upgraded/swapped, the old tokens remain stuck in the contract.

## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps 
- Add a _reclaimExcessTokens function that allows a config owner to withdraw their excess rewards that have accrued.
- Allow the _rescueFunds function to specify the beneficiary, rather than always being the Comptroller admin.
- Automatically sweep excess rewards to config owners on a regular basis.



## Assessed type

Other

issues.title: First Depositor Attack is possible by front-running mip00 script execution
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/test/proposals/mips/mip00.sol#L341-L367
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/test/proposals/mips/mip00.sol#L285-L294


# Vulnerability details

## Overview
### The First Depositor Attack
Within the context of Compound v2, a First Depositor Attack occurs when an attacker becomes the inaugural minter of a cToken. This enables them to establish the first exchange rate between the underlying asset and the cToken. By minting a small amount (1 wei) and subsequently transferring a substantial amount of the underlying asset directly to the cToken contract, the attacker can significantly inflate the exchange rate. As a result, subsequent mints yield a disproportionately small return of cTokens or none at all. The attacker can then redeem their 1 wei cToken for all the underlying assets in that cToken contract.

### The Transaction Execution Process of the Forge Script
The Forge script executes its transactions by simulating the script against the latest state of the blockchain, generating calldatas and nonces according to the calls within the broadcast scope of the script. These prepared transactions are then individually submitted to the blockchain. Since the atomicity of execution can never be assured, the script is exposed to potential front-running and alterations of the on-chain state.

### Cross-chain Governance Through TemporalGovernor
Admin-level functions of contracts on the Base chain are executed via the TemporalGovernor contract. This uses the Wormhole protocol to receive messages from the main governor contract situated on the Moonbeam chain. When a proposal is executed on the Moonbeam governor, a Wormhole message is created and a Validated Action Attestation (VAA) can be obtained. Anyone in possession of the VAA is granted the ability to queue the proposal on the Base chain governor and, once the proposal delay has lapsed, can execute it.

More collateral is  seized outside of the comptroller's approved liquidation amount which means excess seizeTokens are transferred from the borrower to the liquidator leading to loss of funds

liquidateBorrowFresh first checks the allowance of the liquidator: https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/fced18035107a345c31c9a9497d0da09105df4df/src/core/MToken.sol#L970-L973

2. Repays the borrow by calling repayBorrowFresh().
3. Calculates the number of collateral tokens to seize (seizeTokens) based on the actual repay amount.

In step 3, seizeTokens is calculated as 200 tokens
200 tokens are seized even though only 100 were approved
So the vulnerability is:

The comptroller approval happens before the seizeTokens is calculated
If exchange rates change in between, more collateral is seized than approved

An integer overflow could cause the getDerivedPrice() function to return an incorrect price. This could lead to financial losses for users of the contract.

Sure, I can generate a report with this information for all the bugs in the smart contract you provided. Here is an example of a report that I could generate:

contracts/ChainlinkCompositeOracle.sol:120

The getDerivedPrice() function in the ChainlinkCompositeOracle contract uses an integer to represent the price of an asset. However, the function does not check to make sure that the price is within the range of an integer. This could lead to an integer overflow, which could cause the function to return an incorrect price.

The following code shows how an integer overflow could be exploited in the getDerivedPrice() function:

uint256 price = 2**256 - 1;

This code will cause the getDerivedPrice() function to return a value that is different from the input price.

manual code review

issues.title: Users repay more than the approved amount.
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/fced18035107a345c31c9a9497d0da09105df4df/src/core/MToken.sol#L865-L932
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/fced18035107a345c31c9a9497d0da09105df4df/src/core/MToken.sol#L889-L893


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
More tokens can be repaid than were approved leading to loss of funds 

## Proof of Concept
The repayBorrowFresh function does the following:

1. Checks if repay is allowed by calling comptroller.repayBorrowAllowed() with the input repayAmount.
2. Fetches the account's total borrows and sets repayAmount equal to either the input param or total borrows.
3. Transfers repayAmount tokens from the payer.
The issue is that in step 2, the repayAmount is set after the allowance check in step 1. This means if the account's total borrow balance has increased since step 1, the repayAmount could end up higher than the amount approved by the comptroller.

For example:

Comptroller allows a repay of 100 tokens
Between steps 1 and 2, total borrows increases to 120 tokens
In step 2, repayAmount is set to 120 tokens
120 tokens are transferred even though only 100 were approved

## Tools Used
Manual 
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
repayAmount should be set first before calling the comptroller allowance check.

The steps should be:
- Set repayAmount based on input param and total borrows
- Check comptroller.repayBorrowAllowed(repayAmount)
- Transfer repayAmount if allowed


## Assessed type

Other

issues.title: User can bypass their approved redeem allowance
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/fced18035107a345c31c9a9497d0da09105df4df/src/core/MToken.sol#L615-L721


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The caller can bypass the allowance check by exploiting the exchange rate calculation and drain funds from the contract up to the full balance owned by msg.sender, not just the amount approved in the allowance.

## Proof of Concept
The issue is that redeemAmount is calculated after the allowance check. This means if the exchange rate has increased significantly between steps 1 and 2, the actual redeemAmount transferred could be greater than the amount allowed by the comptroller.

For example:

Alice tries to redeem 10 tokens
1 token = 2 USD currently, so 10 tokens = 20 USD
Comptroller allows redeem of up to 20 USD (based on 10 tokens)
Exchange rate has increased to 1 token = 3 USD now
redeemAmount is calculated as 10 tokens * 3 USD per token = 30 USD
So Alice redeems 30 USD worth, even though only allowed 20 USD based on the allowance check

## Tools Used 
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
the redeemAmount should be calculated first, then the comptroller allowance check should happen with redeemAmount as the parameter

Other

issues.title: Unauthorized Admin Transfer Vulnerability
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/src/core/Unitroller.sol#L109


# Vulnerability details

## Description


The bug in this contract is that it doesn't handle the case when the pendingAdmin is set to the zero address (address(0)). As per the condition msg.sender == address(0), the if statement can be bypassed if an attacker sets pendingAdmin to the zero address.

 This is because the condition in the if statement is incorrect:

if (msg.sender != pendingAdmin || msg.sender == address(0)) {
    return fail(Error.UNAUTHORIZED, FailureInfo.ACCEPT_ADMIN_PENDING_ADMIN_CHECK);
}


Here's what's happening in the function:

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/src/core/Oracles/ChainlinkOracle.sol#L97-L113


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Due to an insecure implementation of ChainlinkOracle, in cases of adverse market conditions, users may be able to borrow loans far greater than the intended allowed value. This may result in a business critical risk materialising, collapsing the continued viability of the Moonwell Protocol operations.

Chainlink aggregators have a built-in circuit breaker that kicks in when the price of an asset goes outside of a predetermined price band. This means that in cases of systemic market risk, where an asset experiences a huge drop in value (e.g., the LUNA crash), the price of the oracle will continue to return the minimum price instead of the actual price of the asset. This would allow users to continue borrowing with the asset, but at the wrong price. This is exactly what happened to Venus protocol on BSC when LUNA imploded: https://rekt.news/venus-blizz-rekt/.

```solidity
 (, int256 answer, , uint256 updatedAt, ) = AggregatorV3Interface(feed)
            .latestRoundData();
```

The `latestRoundData` pulls the associated aggregator and requests round data from it. ChainlinkAggregators have minPrice and maxPrice circuit breakers built into them. This means that if the price of the asset falls below the minPrice, the protocol will persist in valuing the token at the minPrice instead of its actual value. This could potentially enable users to take out huge amounts of undercollateralized debt and lead to the bankruptcy of the protocol.

Therefore, in the event of systemic market risk occuring and a regurlarly utlized asset price crashes (e.g., LUNA), the protocol can be manipulated to offer loans of a greater value than should be allowed due to relying on an inccurate and overvalued price of the underlying asset. This poses significant risks to the platform's stability and financial health.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

If an attacker were to change the admin variable to their own address, they would be able to call the _becomeImplementation() function and set the implementation address to their own contract. This would give them control over the MErc20Delegate contract and allow them to perform unauthorized actions, such as transferring tokens or withdrawing funds.

## Proof of Concept

The admin variable is used to control access to the _becomeImplementation() and _resignImplementation() functions. However, the code does not specify how the admin variable is initialized or how it can be changed. This means that it is possible for an attacker to change the admin variable to their own address, which would give them unauthorized access to these functions.

The following code shows how an attacker could change the admin variable and gain unauthorized access to the MErc20Delegate contract:

contract Attacker {
  function changeAdmin(address newAdmin) public {
    MErc20Delegate delegate = MErc20Delegate(0x...);
    delegate.admin = newAdmin;
  }
}

## Tools Used

Manual code inspection and analysis

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The following mitigation steps can be taken to address the vulnerability:

The admin variable should be initialized to a known safe value, such as the address of the contract owner.
The admin variable should be made immutable, so that it cannot be changed after it is initialized.
The admin variable should be protected by a well-established access control mechanism, such as OpenZeppelin's Ownable.

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/fced18035107a345c31c9a9497d0da09105df4df/src/core/Unitroller.sol#L11


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`Unitroller.sol` which is a proxy contract, Has some admin functions and fallback for delegating the calls to implementation contract in this case `Comptroller`.
But there is a problem, in solidity each function is known by its 4 bytes signature and when we want to call a function in real we are calling this signature not the name, there is possibilty two functions with different name and even different parameters have the same function selector, eg: `collate_propagate_storage(bytes16)` and `burn(uint256)` functions has the same 4 bytes identifier of `0x42966c68`. Solidity compiler catches this problem if it happens but not when you are interacting with other contracts.
So by knowing this there is possibility one of the admin functions selector in `Unitroller.sol` has the same function selector with the function that user wants to call in implementation, If that happens their call will never be forwarded to the implementation since that function selector (4 bytes sig) already exist in the proxy contract. (If your current implementation doesn't have this vulnerabilty your future implementations may have this, you shouldn't rely on luck)

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
You can use one of this 2 proxy patterns to prevent this problem:
1. [Transparent proxy](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/api/proxy#TransparentUpgradeableProxy)
2. [UUPSUpgradeable](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/api/proxy#UUPSUpgradeable)
